\section[\hi{ग्यारह} — \hi{बीस}]{\hi{ग्यारह}, \hi{बीस} — genuinely irregular, and one honest exception}

\label{lesson:HI-C22-gyarah-bees}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Be honest about this one: Hindi's teens don't follow a clean, predictable pattern the way Spanish's or Latin's do. But hiding inside that irregularity is a real echo of something you just saw in Latin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The two words — Eleven to twenty}

\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{Hindi} & \textbf{said} \\

\subsection*{The two words — Honest irregularity}
Unlike Spanish's transparent \emph{dieciséis}-\emph{diecinueve} or even the fused-but- regular \emph{once}-\emph{quince}, Hindi's 11-18 each descend from their own Sanskrit number-word (\emph{ekādaśa, dvādaśa, trayodaśa}...) through centuries of individually unpredictable erosion. Most end in \textbf{-rah}, a worn-down echo of Sanskrit's "-daśa" ("ten"), but the erosion of each number's front half isn't predictable from the number itself — these genuinely have to be memorized one by one, the way English speakers just memorize "eleven" and "twelve" rather than deriving them.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{उन्नीस}}
Here's the honest exception: \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} (\emph{unnīs}, 19) most likely isn't simply a worn-down "nine-ten" — it likely continues Sanskrit's \textbf{own} special, \textbf{subtractive} name for 19: \textbf{\hi{ऊनविंशति}} (\emph{ūnaviṃśati}), literally "\textbf{one less than twenty}" (from \emph{ūna}, "less, deficient," + \emph{viṃśati}, "twenty" — a later, shortened form of the fuller Vedic \emph{ekonaviṃśati}, "one-less-twenty," with the \emph{eka}, "one," eventually dropped). Sanskrit used this same \emph{ūna-}/ \emph{ekona-} ("one-less-than") subtractive pattern for every number ending in 9 up through 99 — 29, 49, 99, all named as "one less than" the next round number.

This is a genuine, striking parallel to something you already met: \textbf{Latin's own ūndēvīgintī} ("one from twenty") for 19, from the numbers-11-20 lesson. Two completely unrelated language families — Indo-Aryan and Italic, both descended from Proto-Indo-European but separated for thousands of years — independently landed on the exact same subtractive logic for naming nineteen.

\subsection*{The two words — \hi{बीस}}
\textbf{\hi{बीस}} (\emph{bīs}, "twenty") continues Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{विंशति}} (\emph{viṃśati}, "twenty").

  \item {[}YOU SAY: "unnīs" — 19, most likely "one less than twenty" (ūnaviṃśati), echoing Latin's ūndēvīgintī{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "bīs" — twenty{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Do Hindi's numbers 11-18 follow a predictable pattern the way Spanish's teens do? (\textbf{No} — each is individually eroded from its own Sanskrit ancestor and must be memorized.) What does \textbf{\hi{उन्नीस}} most likely preserve from Sanskrit, and what does it mean? (Sanskrit's \textbf{subtractive} \emph{ūnaviṃśati}, "\textbf{one less than twenty}.") What Latin number from an earlier lesson uses the exact same subtractive logic? (\textbf{ūndēvīgintī}, "one from twenty" — two unrelated language families, the same idea.)
\end{tcolorbox}
